title: A search benchmark has two axes: how low the energy goes, and how many evaluations it cost
summary: The four conformer-search figures compare a reinforcement-learning search with two reference methods on one molecule and one force field. Reading them means separating three things: the best energy found, the average quality of the policy's samples, and the evaluation count paid to get there.

media.alt: Line chart of MMFF94 energy in kcal/mol against REINFORCE training step from 0 to 400. A noisy grey curve starts near 0 and drifts down to about minus 4.4. A blue best-so-far line drops to about minus 6.7 near step 30 and stays flat there, level with a red dashed line at the same value. A green dotted line sits higher, near minus 5.9.

03_02_three_way_benchmark: two bar panels, final energy and force-field evaluation count (log scale) for the three methods
04_03_torsion_convergence: the 11 backbone torsion angles of the best conformer, plotted at each best-so-far update, against the all-anti reference lines at plus and minus 180 degrees
source.note: The project page calls this an honest three-way benchmark. As drawn, the reinforcement-learning method ties the evolution-strategy reference on energy and costs far more evaluations; the figures show that openly. See 'As drawn'.

read_the_figure.question: Does the learning-based search find a conformer as low in energy as the reference methods, and at what cost in force-field evaluations?
read_the_figure.axes: Representative figure: x is REINFORCE training step (0 to 400); y is MMFF94 energy in kcal/mol (about -7 to +0.5), lower is better. The grey line is the mean of each training batch; the blue line is the best energy seen so far; the red dashed and green dotted horizontal lines are the two reference methods' final energies. In the benchmark figure, the left panel is final energy per method and the right panel is evaluation count on a log axis.
look_at: Blue (best-so-far) can only step down, never up. It measures the single best sample ever drawn, not how good the policy has become.
Grey (batch mean) measures the policy itself: the average quality of what it samples now. It keeps improving long after blue has gone flat, then plateaus.
The two horizontal lines are fixed targets, not curves that evolve with training steps. Where blue meets the red line is where the learner has matched that reference.
In the benchmark panels, compare the left panel (quality) with the right panel (cost). A method can tie on the left and lose heavily on the right.
In the torsion figure the markers are the data; the straight segments between them only connect updates and say nothing about what happened between them.
read_the_figure.proves: That, for this molecule and this force field, the learner can reach the same best energy as the reference search. It does not show that the learner is more efficient: best-so-far energy and cost have to be read together.
if_wrong: If the learner's blue line never reaches the references, the policy is not exploring enough or the reward is badly scaled.
If the grey batch mean stays far above blue, the policy has not learned: blue is just luck from many samples.
If the reference lines were drawn from a different force field, or a different number of conformers, the comparison is not like for like.
must_check: All three methods use the same force field (the title says MMFF94) and the same molecule.
Evaluation counts are reported for every method, on the same footing (here, counted as force-field evaluations).
A single run is shown. The spread over random seeds is not drawn, so a gap or a tie is one sample from a distribution.
The all-anti reference is a structural expectation for an unbranched alkane, not the force field's own exact optimum.
as_drawn: Values below are printed on the benchmark figure, or read from the training curve by eye (about 10 percent).

Final MMFF94 energy: RL rotor-tuning -6.713, IPOP-CMA-ES -6.713, ETKDG+MMFF94 -5.890 kcal/mol (printed). The two searches tie; the 200-conformer pipeline is about 0.82 kcal/mol higher (computed: 6.713 - 5.890).

Force-field evaluations: 230,400 for RL, 6,600 for IPOP-CMA-ES, 200 for ETKDG+MMFF94 (printed). RL costs about 35 times the evolution strategy (230,400 / 6,600 = 34.9) and the evolution strategy about 33 times the embedding pipeline (6,600 / 200 = 33). The right panel is a log axis, so the bars understate how large the ratios are.

Training curve: blue reaches the plateau near step 30 (read by eye) and does not move again in 400 steps. The grey batch mean starts near 0 and levels off near -4.4 after roughly step 200, still about 2.3 kcal/mol above blue.

Torsion figure: after the early updates the angles sit at plus or minus 127 to 172 degrees, with a few near -112 to -143. They have moved toward the +/-180 lines but most are not on them at the last point, step 184. The best-so-far update steps shown are 184 at the right edge, while the training curve shows no energy change after about step 30, so later updates must be small; the figure does not give the size.

terms.meaning: One 3D shape of a molecule that differs from another by rotations about single bonds. A long chain such as n-dodecane has a huge number of them.
The twist about one bond, measured between two planes. Around a C-C bond, 180 degrees is the straight, extended (anti) arrangement; around +/-60 is gauche.

A standard molecular-mechanics force field: an energy function of bond lengths, angles, torsions and non-bonded contacts, in kcal/mol. It is the objective being minimised, so it is only as good as the force field.
Every backbone torsion at 180 degrees, the fully extended zig-zag chain. For an unbranched alkane it is the usual textbook ground state in a force field without solvent.
A policy-gradient method: sample actions from a probability distribution, score them, and shift the distribution towards samples with above-average reward.
Best-so-far is the running minimum over every evaluation; the batch mean averages the policy's current samples. They answer different questions: search result versus learning progress.
Covariance-matrix-adaptation evolution strategy with restarts of increasing population size: a derivative-free global optimiser.
RDKit's stochastic conformer generator that uses distance geometry and torsion preferences from crystal data; the output is then relaxed with MMFF94.

remember: Always read quality and cost together: a tie on energy with a 35-fold difference in evaluations is not a tie.
Best-so-far is monotone by construction; it measures luck plus search effort, not learning.
The policy-gradient estimate is the average of (reward minus a baseline) times the gradient of log probability; the baseline lowers variance without changing the expected gradient.
For minimisation, a reward is the negative energy, so a larger reward means a lower energy.
A log-scale bar chart does not show a ratio by bar length; read the labels.

understand.title: Why three methods on one force field
understand.text: Because the force field defines the landscape. If two methods minimise different functions their energies cannot be compared. Here all three use MMFF94, so a difference in final energy is a difference in search quality.

understand.title: Why the batch mean lags the best
understand.text: The learner samples from a spread-out distribution. The best of many draws is much lower than the average draw. Training narrows the distribution, so the average moves towards the best, but exploration noise keeps it above.

steps.title: The score-function (REINFORCE) gradient
steps.note: The gradient of an expected reward can be written as an expectation of reward times the gradient of the log-probability, so it needs only samples and rewards, not derivatives of the energy. Here a is a set of torsion angles and R is the negative MMFF94 energy.

steps.title: A baseline removes variance, not signal
steps.note: Subtracting any constant b leaves the expected gradient unchanged because the expected score is zero. Choosing b near the average reward makes the batch mean the natural centre, which is why the grey curve is the quantity the update works on.

steps.title: Best-so-far is a running minimum
steps.note: It is non-increasing by definition. A curve that steps down early and then stays flat says that no later sample beat the best draw, not that learning stopped.

steps.title: Cost ratio from the printed counts
steps.note: Reading the ratio from the printed numbers is safer than from bar lengths on a log axis. The same arithmetic gives 6,600 / 200 = 33 for the evolution strategy against the embedding pipeline.

steps.title: The structural reference: anti is 180 degrees
steps.note: Because torsion angles are periodic, +180 and -180 are the same state. This is why the torsion figure draws two dashed lines and why a point that jumps from +170 to -170 has not moved far.

worked.title: Cost of reaching the tie, per training step
worked.problem: The benchmark figure prints 230,400 force-field evaluations for the 400 training steps of the training curve. If the batch size is constant, how many evaluations does one step use, and how many evaluations were spent before the best-so-far line stopped moving near step 30?

solution.text: Divide the total by the number of steps.
Multiply by the step at which blue reaches the plateau (read by eye, about 30).

worked.answer: About 576 evaluations per step, so roughly 17,000 evaluations were spent by the time the best energy was found. That is of the same order as the 6,600 used by the evolution strategy, which suggests that most of the learner's budget is spent after the best energy has been found. The step-30 reading is approximate and the constant-batch assumption is mine.

analyze.q: The RL method and IPOP-CMA-ES end at the same energy to three decimals. What does that suggest about the landscape, and what does it not tell you about the difference in the torsion angles?
analyze.hint: Two methods can find the same energy minimum, or two different geometries with similar energy.

analyze.q: The batch mean plateaus near -4.4 while the best stays at -6.7. If you needed a method that reliably produces good conformers in every batch, which curve would you look at?
analyze.hint: Think of best-so-far as a statement about the maximum and the batch mean as a statement about the typical sample.

analyze.q: Most torsions in the last torsion-plot column are not at +/-180, yet the energy ties with the reference. Give two readings of that.
analyze.hint: Is the all-anti line the exact force-field optimum? How are angle values wrapped and sampled?

evaluate.q: Is a learning method that ties on energy and needs 35 times more evaluations a good result? State what it would need to show to justify the cost.
evaluate.hint: Reuse across molecules, transfer to a harder target, or a much cheaper per-molecule cost after training.

evaluate.q: The figures use one molecule and one run. What additional evidence would make the three-way comparison convincing?
evaluate.hint: Seeds, several chain lengths, and a branched molecule where all-anti is not the answer.

create: Redraw the benchmark as one chart: energy gap to the best on the x axis, evaluations on a log y axis, one marker per method, with the multi-seed range as error bars.
Add to the training curve a second x axis in cumulative force-field evaluations, so the learner and the evolution strategy can be drawn on the same cost axis.

checks.q: Why does the best-so-far curve never go up while the batch mean does?
checks.hint: One is a running minimum, the other an average of new samples.
checks.answer: Best-so-far is the minimum over all samples so far, which can only fall or stay. The batch mean averages the current batch, and random sampling noise makes it fluctuate.

checks.q: A method uses 6,600 evaluations and another 230,400. How many times more does the second cost?
checks.answer: 230,400 / 6,600 is about 34.9, so roughly 35 times as many.

checks.q: Both searches reach -6.713 kcal/mol. Does that prove they found the same geometry?
checks.hint: Different geometries can have similar energies, and MMFF94 has symmetric minima.
checks.answer: No. The energy is a single number. Different torsion patterns, or mirror-image conformers, can give the same energy. The torsion figure is the extra evidence about shape.

checks.q: Why is a log-scale bar chart a poor way to show a 35-fold cost difference?
checks.hint: What does bar length mean when the axis does not start at zero?
checks.answer: On a log axis the bar length encodes the logarithm measured from an arbitrary baseline, so the visual ratio between bars is not the real ratio. Print the numbers, or use a dot plot with labelled values.

checks.q: Design one extra panel that would show whether the learner is improving or just lucky.
checks.hint: Consider the spread across seeds and the distribution rather than the extreme.
checks.answer: Plot the batch median and a 10th-90th percentile band against step for several seeds. If the whole band moves down, the policy improved; if only the minimum moves, the result is sampling luck.
